profiles.name: Daniel Crawford
profiles.description: Daniel Crawford was one of the Fort Worth Five, five Irish-American men jailed in Texas in 1972 for refusing to testify before a federal grand jury investigating Irish Republican Army gun-running. The grand jury, sitting in Fort Worth, was probing an alleged scheme to buy weapons in the United States and ship them to the IRA in Northern Ireland. Granted immunity and ordered to testify, Daniel Crawford and his four co-resisters refused, regarding the grand jury as an instrument of political repression against Irish republican solidarity. They were jailed for civil contempt in mid-1972 and held without bail at the Federal Correctional Institution at Seagoville, near Dallas, until their release in September 1972, when they were greeted by relatives and Irish bagpipers at LaGuardia Airport in New York. The case became a cause celebre for Irish-American and civil-liberties supporters opposed to the use of grand juries to investigate political associations.
profiles.query: "Daniel Crawford" Fort Worth Five portrait photograph
profiles.finding: Fort Worth Five court record and Big Spring Herald caption identify Crawford behind Morahan. Newspaper scan remains crop lead.

profiles.name: Chuck Giuli
profiles.description:
Chuck Giuli was a Hawaii anti-war activist associated with catholic Action of Hawaii. He drove participants to the March 2, 1972 Hickam Air Force Base protest, during which Jim Douglass poured blood on electronic-warfare files. Giuli became the third defendant in the Hickam Three prosecution. His charges were dismissed for insufficient evidence connecting him to the destruction of documents.

Sources: https://thestreetspirit.org/2015/06/08/street-spirit-interview-with-james-douglass/ ; https://www.ilind.net/2019/07/01/nuremberg-prosecutor-featured-on-60-minutes-defended-hawaii-peace-activists-in-1972-case/
profiles.finding: Douglass interview confirms Hickam Three role; Ian Lind historical photos remain lead. Contemporary Marimed adviser requires identity continuity before use.

profiles.name: Bernard Coard
profiles.description: Bernard Coard was a Grenadian government or military figure imprisoned in the Grenada Seventeen case following the 1983 U.S. invasion. Amnesty International documents nine to twelve days of incommunicado U.S. military custody before transfer to Grenadian authorities. The group was later convicted in connection with the killings of Maurice Bishop and others. Amnesty classified them as political prisoners and challenged the fairness of their trial without taking a position on guilt or innocence. The final seven members of the group were released in September 2009. Contemporary reports disagree on September 4 versus September 5, so an exact day is not assigned here.
profiles.finding: Grenada identity corroborated; book-signing and archive leads need primary original and rights verification.

profiles.name: Carol Crooks
profiles.description: Carol Crooks was a Black woman imprisoned at the Bedford Hills Correctional Facility for Women in New York who became a central figure in the 1970s women's prison movement. Jailed as a teenager on a first-degree manslaughter conviction and sentenced to up to 15 years in 1972, she sued over being thrown into solitary confinement without notice or a hearing and won a July 1974 ruling establishing incarcerated women's right to due process before segregation (Crooks v. Warne). On August 29, 1974, after she was involved in a brief fight, a squad of male guards in riot gear from a nearby prison forced into her cell, beat her, and dragged her out — provoking the "August Rebellion," an uprising by some 200 women who took over parts of the prison in protest of her treatment; the women later won the class-action suit Powell v. Ward. The Black Panther reported in early 1980 that Crooks, after years of fighting conditions at Bedford Hills and serving as a lead plaintiff in suits over illegal segregation transfers and inadequate medical care, had just been sentenced in Westchester to a further three-and-a-half to fifteen years on an in-prison assault charge, and — instead of a long-overdue parole she had been told she had won — was told she must serve three more years before becoming parole-eligible.
profiles.finding: Spectre Journal explicitly labels Carol Crooks image from Dyke Quarterly; Village Voice and Freedom Archives corroborate. Original resolution and credit check pending.

profiles.name: Mark Edward Allen
profiles.description: Mark Edward Allen was thirteen years old when Monrovia, California, police arrested him on suspicion of shoplifting a leather coat on November 16, 1971. Police booked Allen at 5:11 p.m. and confined him in cell M4 at the Monrovia Police Station. Officers reported finding him unresponsive at about 6:25 p.m. and said he had strangled himself with his pants. A Black police cadet said Allen had arrived shirtless, highly agitated and scratched across his body. Allen was pronounced dead at Arcadia Methodist Hospital. He spent a little more than one hour in the station before he was found unresponsive.
profiles.finding: Hey SoCal confirms thirteen-year-old Monrovia victim; Canadian veteran born1961 rejected.

profiles.name: Charles Pernasilice

profiles.name: John Grady
profiles.description:
John Grady was an auto mechanic from Ithaca, NY and patriarch of the Grady family of Catholic radicals. He had previously been a defendant in the Camden 28 anti-draft action of 1971 and worked closely with Daniel and Philip Berrigan; his daughters Clare, Ellen, and Teresa Grady all became major Plowshares and Catholic Worker activists. The Grady family home in Ithaca was a center of Vietnam-era and ongoing antiwar organizing.

Veteran Catholic peace activist and labor organizer, considered an organizational leader of the Camden 28 draft-board raid of August 21–22, 1971. Acquitted with all other tried defendants in the landmark May 1973 jury-nullification verdict in Camden, New Jersey.

profiles.description: Age 23 at indictment; Boston Technical School graduate and former VISTA volunteer in Appalachia. A member of the 'Boston 8', sentenced (suspended) for refusing to carry his draft cards, and charged with criminal contempt for refusing to answer the Harrisburg Grand Jury. Acquitted with the Camden 28 in 1973.
profiles.finding: PBS POV trial excerpt identifies Paul Couming second from left; press photo lead. Actor Craig Archibald portrayal and older priest namesake rejected.

profiles.name: Terry Buckalew
profiles.description: Age 21 at indictment; valedictorian of Wildwood Catholic High School, NJ, and recipient of a John F. Kennedy award for courage and moral integrity. Attended Rider College and worked as a court clerk in the Federal Third Circuit of Appeals. Had refused induction into the armed forces. Acquitted in 1973.
profiles.finding: Camden press kit, NARA arrest record and spouse memoir match; no usable individual image verified.

profiles.name: Joan Reilly
profiles.description: Age 20 at indictment; from Brightwaters, Long Island, a psychology/philosophy junior at Marymount College, Tarrytown, and elected student senator. Volunteered with the Christian Appalachian Project. Acquitted in 1973.
profiles.finding: PBS POV labels Joan Reilly then/now, but inspected modern thumbnail only60x60. Weavers Way October2008 captioned photo remains lead.

profiles.name: Peter Fordi
profiles.description: Jesuit priest, age 35 at indictment, based at Woodstock Religious College, NYC; native of Jersey City who entered the Society of Jesus in 1956. Had already taken public responsibility (with the East Coast Conspiracy to Save Lives) for the February 1970 Philadelphia draft-board and Washington GE-office raids. At trial he declared 'I ripped up those files with my hands.' Acquitted in 1973.
profiles.finding: Camden press kit and Catholic Peace Fellowship corroborate; historical group image needs explicit position and crop verification.
